Such competitive pressures are likely to impact entire supply chains, from critical material mining to finished products. For example, expected increases in deep-sea mining due to increasing critical mineral demand, driven in part by advanced energy technology proliferation, will likely impact U.S. Navy operations and maritime norms. To help offset these pressures, DOW can invest in research and development of cost-effective, resource-efficient technologies that reduce dependence on scarce or strategically contested materials. Associated supply shortages and rising prices will impact DOW even more for those materials that are also critical to other defense applications. For instance, antimony is used to improve the efficiency of perovskite solar cells (Guo et al. 2023), and it also plays a critical role in military applications such as flame-retardant materials, armor-piercing ammunition, and explosives (New Age Metals Inc. 2025). Working with partners to increase the domestic production of key materials and components could be key to maintaining supply, although higher costs are harder to mitigate. 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 5 Uncertainties Several uncertainties could unfold within the 20-year time horizon used for this report that could amplify or reduce the risks outlined. Risks that are not evident today could become more apparent as the adoption of advanced energy technologies accelerates and as more nations rely on these assets for both civilian and defense energy needs. 5.1 Technological Innovations Some technological innovations could facilitate the deployability of advanced energy technologies, creating opportunities and risks. For example, radio frequency or optical power beaming and the potential to move bulk power generation to space could enable DOW operations worldwide but also shift DOW’s strategic focus toward defending space-based and aerial systems. The United Kingdom is considering uncrewed space assets for power delivery, which could alter the future landscape of military operations (U.K. Ministry of Defence 2023). The adoption of terrestrial or space-based power beaming would likely benefit militaries with relatively more electrified assets. Market-driven innovations will likely continue to reduce the cost and amount of materials required for advanced energy systems. For example, innovative batteries and motors for EVs are being developed to avoid rare earth materials, reduce size and weight, and increase power density. Although this example aligns with DOW goals, innovation driven predominantly by commercial rather than military needs and interests could result in solutions not fully suitable for military applications. The gaps might not be clear without testing, failures, and modifications. 5.2 Changes in Supply Chain Efforts to secure increasing supplies of advanced energy inputs could have other impacts. For example, deep-sea mining for lithium and other critical minerals could impact the broader security environment and therefore DOW priorities. Supply chain uncertainty also stems from the complex interactions between advanced energy supply chains and technological developments.
